sentences.text: Estimates for the animal's size vary, with some sources suggesting it reached 5 meters in length and weighed 1.3 tonnes, while others estimate a length of approximately 4.5 meters.
Its skull measured about 370.3 millimeters long and 299.1 millimeters wide, narrowing to 203.7 millimeters at the rear.
A unique feature of this dinosaur is a quadrate bone that is shorter and wider than in any other known ankylosaur.
The vertebrae were amphicoelous, meaning they were wider than they were tall and constricted in the middle.
The sacrum, a series of fused vertebrae at the base of the spine, was arched dorsally by 55 degrees.
Like other nodosaurids, it possessed a foot with four pedal phalanges.
Europelta is the largest known member of the dinosaur clade Struthiosaurini.
Hollow, plate-like osteoderms with sharp edges ran down the sides of its tail and decreased in size rapidly.
The femoral head is angled at approximately 115 degrees relative to the femur's long axis.
The tibia features a broadly rounded cnemial crest.
The genus Europelta and the species Europelta carbonensis were named by James I. Kirkland, Luis Alcalá, Mark A. Loewen, Eduardo Espílez, Luis Mampel, and Jelle P. Wiersma in 2013.
Two partial skeletons were discovered in 2011.
The holotype and paratype specimens were found with abundant osteoderms, but these were not preserved in their original positions relative to the skeleton.
Microfossils indicate that the habitat was a permanent freshwater lake.
The fossil-bearing layer consists of dark olive-gray to olive-black mudstone preserving a high percentage of fossil plant debris.
Evidence of fused fern lamellae and abundant charcoal indicates the area was affected by a wildfire.
Heavy rainfall likely moved charred remains downstream where they were later buried in a nearby depositional area.
Europelta is a monospecific genus of nodosaurid dinosaur found in Spain.
Europelta lived during the mid-Cretaceous, specifically the early Albian stage, approximately 113 million years ago, with the stage ranging from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.
Fossils were found in the lower Escucha Formation of the Teruel Province in Spain, specifically in the lower zone of the formation in northeastern Spain.
It is debated whether Europelta belongs to Struthiosaurinae, as the original classification lacked a phylogenetic analysis.
Researchers disagree on Europelta's closest relatives, with some studies placing it as sister to Pawpawsaurus and others including Borealopelta in that relationship.
Some phylogenetic analyses place Europelta in a polytomy with Struthiosaurus, Stegopelta, Hungarosaurus, and Pawpawsaurus.
Other studies suggest Europelta is the sister taxon to Hungarosaurus.
